ety.text: From Middle English fighten (“to fight”), from Old English feohtan (“to fight, combat, strive”), from Proto-West Germanic *fehtan (“to fight”), from Proto-Germanic *fehtaną (“to comb, tease, shear, struggle with”), from Proto-Indo-European *peḱ- (“to comb, shear”).

From Middle English fight, feyght, fiȝt, fecht, from Old English feoht, ġefeoht (“fight”), from Proto-West Germanic *fehtan (“to fight”), from Proto-Germanic *fehtą, *gafehtą (“fight, struggle”), from Proto-Germanic *fehtaną (“to struggle with”). Cognate with Dutch gevecht (“fight”), German Gefecht (“fight”).

senses.d: To engage in combat with; to oppose physically, to contest with.
ex: My grandfather fought the Nazis in World War II.

senses.d: To conduct or engage in (battle, warfare, a cause, etc.).
ex: Our soldiers fought the battle just over that hill.
I have fought a good fight.

senses.d: To contend in physical conflict, either singly or in war, battle, etc.
ex: A wounded animal will fight tooth and nail; relentless, savage and murderous.

senses.d: To contend in physical conflict with each other, either singly or in war, battle, etc.
ex: The two boxers have been fighting for more than half an hour.

senses.d: To cause to fight; to manage or manoeuvre in a fight.
ex: to fight cocks; to fight one’s ship

senses.d: To strive for something; to campaign or contend for success.
ex: He fought for the Democrats in the last election.

senses.d: To try to overpower; to fiercely counteract.
ex: The government pledged to fight corruption.
I fought a sneeze as Max took my hand and led me into the chapel.

senses.d: Of colours or other design elements: to clash; to fail to harmonize.
ex: The higher the saturation, the more the colors fight, and the more users will be looking at your design instead of your content.

senses.d: An occasion of fighting.
ex: One of them got stuck in a chokehold and got stabbed to death during the fight.

senses.d: A battle between opposing armies.
A physical confrontation or combat between two or more people or groups.
ex: Watch your language! Are you looking for a fight?

senses.d: A boxing or martial arts match.
ex: I’m going to Nick’s to watch the big fight tomorrow night.

senses.d: A conflict, possibly nonphysical, with opposing ideas or forces; strife.
ex: I’ll put up a fight to save this company.

senses.d: The will or ability to fight.
ex: That little guy has a bit of fight in him after all. As soon as he saw the size of his opponent, all the fight went out of him.

senses.d: A screen for the combatants in ships; an arming.

ety.text: From Middle English figure, borrowed from Old French figure, from Latin figūra (“form, shape, form of a word, a figure of speech, Late Latin a sketch, drawing”), from fingō (“to form, shape, mold, fashion”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeyǵʰ- (“to mold, shape, form, knead”). Cognate with Ancient Greek τεῖχος (teîkhos), Sanskrit देग्धि (dégdhi), Old English dāg (“dough”). More at dough. Doublet of figura.

senses.d: A drawing or diagram conveying information.
The representation of any form, as by drawing, painting, modelling, carving, embroidering, etc.; especially, a representation of the human body.
ex: a figure in bronze; a figure cut in marble
a coin that bears the figure of an angel

senses.d: A person, thing, or action representative of another
The appearance or impression made by the conduct or career of a person.
ex: He cut a sorry figure standing there in the rain.
I made some figure there.

senses.d: Distinguished appearance; magnificence; conspicuous representation; splendour; show.
ex: that he may live in figure and indulgence

senses.d: A human figure, which dress or corset must fit to; the shape of a human body.
ex: She was cunningly dressed in a black, sheer gown with gold ornaments showing her figure to perfection.

senses.d: A numeral.
A number, an amount.
A shape.
ex: a geometrical figure, a plane figure, a solid figure
Flowers have all exquisite figures.

senses.d: A visible pattern as in wood or cloth.
ex: The muslin was of a pretty figure.

senses.d: To calculate, to solve a mathematical problem.
To come to understand.
ex: I can’t figure if he’s telling the truth or lying.

senses.d: To think, to assume, to suppose, to reckon.
ex: We can figure on running a loss this year.

1. Gent. Thou art alwayes figuring diseases in me; but
thou art full of error, I am sound.

senses.d: To be reasonable or predictable.
ex: It figures that somebody like him would be upset about the situation.

senses.d: To enter into; to be a part of.
ex: It is the transcontinental trains which figure most prominently in railway advertising. Both railways run two trains in each direction.
The exchange rate figures heavily in several other aspects of Venezuela's economy.

senses.d: To represent in a picture or drawing.
To represent by a figure, as to form or mould; to make an image of, either palpable or ideal; also, to fashion into a determinate form; to shape.
ex: If love, alas! be pain; the pain I bear, / No thought can figure, and no tongue declare.

senses.d: To embellish with design; to adorn with figures.
ex: The vaulty top of heaven / Figured quite o'er with burning meteors.

senses.d: To indicate by numerals.

1698 , John Dryden, Epitaph of Mary Frampton

senses.d: To represent by a metaphor; to signify or symbolize.

senses.d: The fruit of the fig tree, pear-shaped and containing many small seeds.
A fruit-bearing tree or shrub of the genus Ficus that is native mainly to the tropics.
ex: And the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked; and they sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons.

senses.d: The value of a fig, practically nothing; a fico; a whit.
ex: I'll pledge you all; and a fig for Peter!

senses.d: A Lady Finger banana, also known as the "fig banana", (cultivar of Musa acuminata)

senses.d: A small piece of tobacco.
ex: “You may flog, and welcome, master,” said he, “if you'll give me a fig o' tibbacky.”

senses.d: A fico, a contemptuous gesture.
To insult with a fico, a contemptuous gesture.
ex: When Pistol lies, do this, and fig me like / The bragging Spaniard.

To develop, or cause (a soap) to develop, white streaks or granulations.
To move suddenly or quickly; rove about.

To dress; to get oneself up a certain way.
